questions.prompt: How does Redis Cluster decide which node holds a key?

options.text: Consistent hashing over a ring
The key maps to one of 16384 hash slots via CRC16(key) mod 16384, and each primary owns a range of slots
A random node is chosen per key
The client always uses node 0

questions.explanation: Cluster uses 16384 fixed hash slots; a key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384, and each primary owns a subset of slots. This is fixed-slot sharding, not consistent hashing.

questions.prompt: What does a MOVED redirect indicate?

options.text: The slot has permanently relocated to another node; update your map and retry there
The key was deleted
The cluster is read-only
A temporary hint for one request during migration

questions.explanation: MOVED means the slot now lives on the named node (a stable relocation). ASK, by contrast, is the temporary during-migration redirect.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Redis Cluster are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Multi-key commands require all keys to be in the same slot
Hash tags {...} force keys to hash to the same slot
Cluster supports the multiple-database SELECT feature
Cluster is not strongly consistent

questions.explanation: Multi-key ops need same-slot keys (hash tags help), and Cluster is async/not strongly consistent. Cluster uses only database 0 — SELECT for multiple DBs is not available.

questions.prompt: Why does `MGET user:1:name user:1:age` sometimes return a CROSSSLOT error in a cluster?

options.text: MGET is not allowed in clusters at all
The two keys may hash to different slots, so no single node can serve them together
The keys are too large
The cluster is out of memory

questions.explanation: A multi-key command needs all keys in one slot. Without a hash tag the two keys can land in different slots, producing CROSSSLOT. Using {user:1} in both key names co-locates them.

questions.prompt: To force related keys into the same slot, wrap a shared substring of the key name in ______ (the two characters that delimit a hash tag).
questions.explanation: A hash tag is a substring inside { } — only that part is hashed, so {user:42}:name and {user:42}:cart share a slot.

questions.prompt: When is Redis Cluster the right choice over Sentinel?

options.text: Whenever you want any failover at all
When your data or write throughput exceeds a single node and you need to shard
When you need multiple logical databases
When you need strong consistency

questions.explanation: Cluster's job is horizontal sharding across nodes. If data fits one node, Sentinel is simpler; Cluster neither adds strong consistency nor multiple databases.
